Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Clinical summary from transcript:
  - 35-year-old male with several-week history of intermittent frontal headaches (often at work/while on computer or in meetings), associated with mild nausea.
  - Episodic palpitations (~once/day, possibly more), subjective feeling of rapid heartbeat.
  - Episodes of feeling hot and shortness of breath occurring while sitting at desk; bilateral hand tingling described as "quick picking" (no lower limb symptoms).
  - Decreased appetite, unintentional 5 lb weight loss, decreased libido; onset temporally related to job change and increased work stress.
  - Past medical history of "hyperthyroidism"; taking thyroxine (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - No tobacco or recreational drug use reported.
  - Patient agreeable to in-person clinic assessment and blood tests.
- Diagnostic reasoning (DDx elements consistent with transcript and incorporated):
  - Thyrotoxicosis (iatrogenic overreplacement or uncontrolled hyperthyroidism) — High likelihood:
    - Supported by history of thyroid disease, current thyroxine use, and multiple sympathetic symptoms (palpitations, heat intolerance/feeling hot, weight loss, decreased libido).
    - DDx emphasizes need for thyroid function testing and medication review.
    - Conflict noted: patient reports "hyperthyroidism" yet is on thyroxine (possible misstatement, treatment for hypothyroidism, or iatrogenic overreplacement) — requires clarification and lab confirmation.
  - Anxiety disorder / Panic attacks (work-related) — High likelihood:
    - Symptoms temporally linked to work/meetings, high reported stress (7–8/10), and episodic shortness of breath, palpitations, paresthesias are consistent with anxiety/panic presentations.
  - Tension-type / cervicogenic headache related to workplace ergonomics — Moderate likelihood:
    - Frontal headaches occurring during prolonged computer/meeting work and onset after job change are consistent with posture-related headache; bilateral hand paresthesias may also be related to repetitive computer use.
  - Cardiac arrhythmia (paroxysmal SVT or other) — possible contributor (DDx raises as medium likelihood); no objective cardiac data yet to confirm.
- Conflicts/uncertainties:
  - Conflict noted between stated diagnosis ("hyperthyroidism") and current medication (thyroxine) — needs clarification and thyroid function tests.
  - No vital signs, ECG, or laboratory data recorded in transcript to confirm arrhythmia or biochemical thyrotoxicosis.

Management Plan
- management_plan_main_or_not_recorded:
  - Arrange in-person clinic appointment for physical examination (focused cardiac and respiratory exam) and medication review.
  - Order thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4 as appropriate) to assess for overreplacement or uncontrolled thyroid disease.
  - Do not commence new medications until in-person review and results available.
  - Review thyroxine dosing and adherence at the visit (dose/route/frequency not documented in record).
  - Consider ECG and ambulatory cardiac monitoring if palpitations persist or if exam/ECG suggests arrhythmia.
  - Address workplace stress and consider evaluation/support for anxiety (discuss nonpharmacologic strategies and mental health referral if indicated).
  - Consider ergonomic assessment if headaches and hand paresthesias persist.
  - Refer to endocrinology if thyroid function tests abnormal; refer to cardiology if arrhythmia detected; consider mental health services for anxiety management.

- Thyrotoxicosis (iatrogenic overreplacement or uncontrolled hyperthyroidism) — High likelihood
  - Justification: History of thyroid disease and current thyroxine use with sympathetic symptoms (palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, decreased libido); DDx supports urgent thyroid function testing and medication review.
  - Conflict noted: inconsistency between reported "hyperthyroidism" and being on thyroxine requires clarification.
- Anxiety disorder / Panic attacks (work-related) — High likelihood
  - Justification: Symptoms commonly triggered by work/meetings, high occupational stress, and episodic nature of autonomic symptoms (palpitations, shortness of breath, paresthesias).
- Tension-type / cervicogenic headache related to ergonomics — Moderate likelihood
  - Justification: Frontal headaches occurring during prolonged computer/meeting work and new onset after job change; bilateral hand paresthesias may relate to repetitive posture or nerve irritation.
